implementation_notes: The JDK keeps the size/capacity split on its array-backed collections: ArrayList.trimToSize() 'Trims the capacity of this ArrayList instance to the list's current size. An application can use this operation to minimize the storage of an ArrayList instance', and Vector, StringBuilder and StringBuffer carry the same call. Capacity is not part of the List/Collection interfaces - only the concrete classes expose it, alongside ensureCapacity for growing - so the trim requires the implementation type, and code that holds a List must either keep a concrete reference or rebuild. When the container is finished rather than merely oversized, the alternative is a right-sized or unmodifiable snapshot (List.copyOf, new ArrayList<>(src)), which retires the original container entirely; note that HashMap/Hashtable have no equivalent, so their bucket table stays at the peak after mass removal.
pitfalls: trimToSize() lives on the concrete classes, not on List/Collection, so code behind a List reference cannot call it - and wrapping (Collections.unmodifiableList, a sublist) hides the method while still sharing the storage.

It reallocates and copies (O(n) plus a second array the size of the survivors), and ArrayList is not thread-safe: running it while another thread iterates or mutates risks ConcurrentModificationException or a torn iteration.

Immutable and copy-on-write collections are a different animal: List.copyOf/List.of snapshots never grow but expose no capacity, and CopyOnWriteArrayList already copies on every write, so 'trimming' it means nothing.
sources: docs.oracle.com, java.util.ArrayList (Java SE 21) - 'Trims the capacity of this ArrayList instance to be the list's current size. An application can use this operation to minimize the storage of an ArrayList instance', next to the class description of capacity/ensureCapacity and the unsynchronized, fail-fast warnings: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/ArrayList.html
